claims.text: 3D ink extrusion printing, hydrogen de-binding, and vacuum sintering with a titanium sponge getter will improve the oxidation resistance of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr while preserving its mechanical performance.
The feedstock is an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr blend of HfH2, NbH, TaH0.5, TiH2, ZrH2, and metallic Ti/Nb in a polystyrene/binder matrix.
The proposed process uses flowing-hydrogen de-binding followed by vacuum sintering at 1400 °C for 18 hours with titanium sponge as an oxygen getter.
The required processing vacuum is below 3×10^-6 torr.
The material is to be water-quenched from approximately 1500 °C.
The proposed protection is applicable in air near 1000 °C for exposures up to 5 hours.
Differences in formation enthalpy cause sequential decomposition of the Ta, Nb, Hf, Ti, and Zr hydrides during processing.
Sequential hydride decomposition facilitates in-situ alloying and oxygen scavenging.
The process results in controlled oxygen uptake of approximately 1.0 wt.% and formation of oxygen-stabilized phases.
Controlled oxygen uptake produces interstitial strengthening.
A silicide coating and titanium sponge lead to formation of a self-healing (Zr,Hf)O2 layer.
The proposed self-healing oxide layer reduces oxygen diffusion and protects the alloy from rapid oxidation.
The processed alloy will be nearly fully dense and will have a metastable single beta-BCC phase.
The processed alloy will have enhanced high-temperature compression strength.
The processed alloy will oxidize significantly more slowly than cast or uncoated HfNbTaTiZr.
Untreated HfNbTaTiZr has a reported oxidation-rate parameter of approximately 570 mg^2 cm^-4 h^-1.
Cast or uncoated sintered HfNbTaTiZr exhibits cracking, alpha-HCP embrittlement, and rapid oxidation under similar conditions.
Maintaining oxygen near 1.0 wt.% and quenching sufficiently rapidly suppresses alpha-HCP formation.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies sintering at 1400 °C, whereas the conditions state that this heating is followed by quenching from approximately 1500 °C; no additional heating step to 1500 °C is defined.
The mechanism depends on a silicide coating, but no silicide coating or silicon-bearing step is included in the stated intervention.

The hypothesis characterizes the intervention primarily as incorporation of a vacuum-sintering step, while the detailed intervention is a multi-step replacement manufacturing route comprising new feedstock preparation, 3D printing, hydrogen de-binding, getter-assisted sintering, and quenching.
